title: EXPLORE YOUR SERVICE IDEA WITH CHATGPT
content:
Now that you have a service idea and a rough idea of how it could be delivered, it is time to pressure-test the concept before packaging it into an offer.

PRESSURE-TEST THE WORK ITSELF
"Help small businesses with social media" could mean strategy, photography, video editing, writing, posting, responding to comments, reporting, or all of them. Those versions require very different time and skills. Define what you actually intend to do.

CHECK CAPACITY BEFORE REVENUE FANTASIES
If one client requires ten hours each month and you have twenty billable hours available, your capacity is not fifty monthly clients. You do not need perfect numbers yet, but you need enough realism to know what must eventually be measured.

PRESSURE-TEST QUESTIONS
If five customers bought this next week, what exactly would you have to do?
What would each customer need from you?
What could go wrong?
Which part consumes the most time?
Which skill is most important?
What would you need before accepting customer one?
Which facts are you currently assuming rather than knowing?

If those answers make the service less appealing, that is useful information before you build around it.

PRESSURE-TEST THE WORK, NOT JUST THE IDEA

A service can sound attractive until you picture the actual Tuesday afternoon version of delivering it.

Use this interview to make the work concrete. What happens before the appointment or project? What information do you need? What do you physically or mentally do? How long might it take? What equipment, software, travel, preparation, follow-up, or customer communication is involved? What happens when several customers need you at once?

This is not a demand-validation exercise and it is not a sales plan. It is a reality check on whether you would actually want and be able to perform the service you are considering.

EXAMPLE: PRESSURE-TESTING A REMOTE BOOKKEEPING IDEA

"I could do bookkeeping" sounds plausible but hides most of the actual work.

A useful exploration asks which bookkeeping tasks you are qualified to perform, what software you know, what records a client would need to provide, how often work occurs, what happens when records are incomplete, how communication works, how many hours a typical account might require, what deadlines exist, what work is explicitly outside scope, and whether any legal, tax, licensing, privacy, insurance, or professional requirements need external verification.

Then imagine three clients arriving at once. Can you onboard all three? What information bottlenecks the work? What happens at month-end? Which parts require judgment and which are routine?

You are not trying to prove the service will succeed. You are converting a pleasant-sounding idea into work you can picture yourself actually doing.

WHAT A PRESSURE TEST IS SUPPOSED TO DO

Pressure-testing is not trying to talk you out of your idea.

It is asking the idea to survive contact with ordinary reality.

Who supplies the information you need? What happens when they are late? What does a normal customer require? What does a difficult customer require? Which part takes longer than expected? What happens when three customers need the same deadline? What mistakes would be costly? What qualifications or protections matter? What would make the service unprofitable or miserable to deliver?

An idea that still appeals to you after those questions is more useful than an idea that only sounded good while it was vague.

QUALIFICATIONS AND PROFESSIONAL BOUNDARIES

A service idea can sound operationally simple while still carrying licensing, certification, insurance, privacy, tax, legal, financial, safety, or other professional requirements depending on the work and jurisdiction.

ChatGPT can help you figure out what questions to investigate. It cannot prove that you are legally qualified, properly insured, or allowed to provide a regulated service.

HOW TO USE THIS
Use the prompt below to turn this branch into your version of the business. Answer the questions honestly, ask for clarification when you need it, and do not treat external facts as verified just because ChatGPT mentions them.

WHAT THIS INTERVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE

By the end, you should understand how the proposed service works in ordinary delivery, where it is likely to become difficult, what capacity it requires, what mistakes matter, and which assumptions need real-world verification.

ChatGPT should actively look for failure points without turning the exercise into automatic pessimism.

At the end, separate problems you can design around from problems serious enough to weaken the service idea.

COPY & PASTE INTO CHATGPT

During the interview:
- Ask one question at a time unless a small group of tightly related questions is genuinely easier to answer together.
- Use my answers before deciding what to ask next. Do not run through a generic questionnaire when an answer makes a question irrelevant.
- If I say "I don't know," help me identify what I need to decide or research. Do not silently invent an answer for me.
- Explain unfamiliar business terms in plain language when they first become relevant.
- Separate assumptions from facts that require outside verification.
- Do not turn this into a marketing or customer-acquisition plan unless the purpose of this specific interview requires it.
- When you have enough information, stop interviewing me and give me the requested conclusion, including the important unknowns and next research questions.
Ask me one question at a time unless a small group of closely related questions would be easier to answer together. If I say I don't know, help me identify what I would need to decide or research instead of inventing an answer for me.

Interview me about my service idea. Ask who the customer is, what problem they have, the result they want, what I would actually do, what skills and tools are required, how I would deliver it, how much time each customer requires, my capacity, direct costs, and how often customers need the service.

Use my answers to test whether one-off or ongoing, custom or standardized, local or remote, and individual or group delivery make sense. Help me identify competitor, pricing, credential, licensing, insurance, and demand questions that require outside research.

Do not invent market demand or tell me the economics work without numbers. End with a service concept specific enough to turn into an offer and a list of unresolved research.

NEXT → PDF 44 if the concept still appeals; PDF 42 if it needs reshaping.

While interviewing me, follow these rules:

Pressure-test the actual work, not just whether the idea sounds appealing. Ask enough operational questions that hidden scope becomes visible.

If the user gives an income goal, do not simply divide it by an invented price. Identify capacity, direct costs, realistic billable time, and pricing research still needed.

At the end, give me:
- Customer
- Problem/result
- Exact work performed
- Delivery shape
- Approximate capacity questions
- Direct-cost questions
- Skills/tools required
- External research
- Specific service direction
